Machine learning models with probabilistic elements, especially those informed by differential equations, offer significant advantages in analyzing complex data sets.  However, working with these models can be challenging, and it can sometimes be difficult to strike a balance between their interpretability and accuracy.  Graph neural networks have emerged as a useful tool for learning patterns from data, but when combined with deep learning models, they can risk overcomplicating underlying processes.  To address these issues, we've developed two novel GNN models that draw inspiration from stochastic differential equations.  By integrating statistical properties and continuity into learning, these models enhance our understanding of data occurring across various domains.  To train these models, we've created a loss function that combines chance-based elements with traditional supervision, allowing us to strike a balance between accuracy and interpretability.  Our proposed models were tested on two challenging datasets, comparing their performance against state-of-the-art models in terms of accuracy and complexity.

The completeness of the lowest degree Appell polynomial is established, enabling the creation of novel, low-degree nonlinearities for vectorial Boolean functions based on this finding. The resulting nonlinearities are classified as slim Sidon sets, a concept initially introduced by the authors in a previous work. The efficiency of these nonlinearities is measured not only by their degree but also by their Appellation polynomial degree and slimness. The relevance of slim Sidon sets is further explained in terms of side-channel attacks, particularly power analysis. The definition of a new class of slim Sidon sets is proposed, derived from a specific type of weakly complete higher degree cross-completeness. The authors' approach allows for the direct generation of efficient, slim Sidon sets using the completeness of Appell polynomials. Additionally, it is proven that slim Sidon sets yield the best vectorial nonlinearities for Boolean functions with an even number of variables.

We investigate the probability distribution of binary matrices with unrestricted entries, subject to a fixed constraint on row and column element sums. To sample from this matrix ensemble, a two-stage process is employed: first, a valid degree sequence is generated, and then, given this degree sequence, a matrix is created. The matrix generation involves dealing with dependencies between entries, which can be addressed using novel methods. These methods include a new 'switching approach' and 'inversion methods' that reveal the matrix's internal structure based on a degree sequence, and 'rejection methods' that show the effectiveness of rejection in specific scenarios. Notably, our findings indicate that rejection may actually increase computational complexity due to the high likelihood of rejection at the initial stages.

In hadron collider experiments, physicists utilize PDFs to model the internal structure of protons, which is essential for interpreting data and interpreting data in line with the Standard Model and exploring potential new phenomena in high-energy physics. PDFs are not inherent parts of the Standard Model, which means they need to be determined through specific mathematical calculations and further refined through further analysis. Fitting processes are utilized to determine the PDFs and which involves combining theoretical predictions with experimental data, which is based on the framework of quantum field theory. This chapter delves into the theorems that form the foundation of PDF fitting by examining matrix elements and scattering amplitudes. It also discusses the framework used for calculating cross-sections and which is grounded in quantum field theory. By examining the framework from both numerical and algebraic perspectives, this chapter provides insights into the foundation of PDF fitting, which is rooted in quantum field theory.

This document details the latest open-source collection of algorithms, with features in virtualization, cloud computing, and high-speed access. Our user-friendly platform offers a wide range of high-quality algorithms for data analysis tasks, including dimensionality reduction, clustering, anomaly detection, and feature selection. In addition to providing well-documented algorithms for common data analysis methods, our repository also includes unique, cutting-edge techniques. To enhance usability and promote collaboration, our team has developed high-level modules for algorithm combination and optimization, as well as efficient data loaders and data manipulation tools for common data formats. Also included are standard evaluation protocols and frameworks to support the common data analysis workflow of evaluation and visualization. This article serves as a continuously-updated catalog of algorithms and functionality within our algorithm collection, with periodic releases of stabilized versions, with the latest being version 0.7.5 along with features in virtualization, cloud computing and named Heidelberg.

We introduce a novel approach to generating a microresonator optical frequency comb using periodic amplitude modulations of the pump laser's amplitude, in lieu of the traditional method relying on phase modulation. The influence of these modulations results in the creation of primary and secondary sidebands around a single laser frequency, facilitating the development of a lockstep frequency comb through a process of four-wave mixing. The use of high-Q, small-radius silicon nitride microresonators allows for the generation of thousands of comb lines within a single gigahertz range. The proposed approach offers increased versatility in tuning comb features and produces cleaner spectral profiles, in contrast to the conventional method.

We establish the existence of countably infinite sets of RGIs for non-virtually cyclic, acylindrically hyperbolic groups that are both distal and loyal, provided at least one such RGI exists. This finding is rooted in the construction of a distal and loyal random subgroup based on a random weak backtracking subgroup of such groups. An expansion on this includes an introduction to hyperbolicity theory not previously covered in handbooks.

This research delves into the generalization capabilities of binary weight neural networks, particularly in the context of overparameterized systems. Theoretical frameworks have been developed to explain the statistical behavior of these networks: an approximate natural theorem has been proposed for systems with discrete weights near specific parameters, and a more rigorous approach has been taken with the quantization theorem. The findings indicate that the generalization of binary weight networks is tied to their ability to separate training examples, which in turn is linked to their high-degree binary Walsh Fourier coefficients. The robustness of this approximate natural theorem has been shown, and it provides a basis for understanding the empirical observations regarding overparameterized binary neural networks. Furthermore, the study examines the computational complexity of evaluating high-degree binary Walsh coefficients, and its implications on generalization are discussed, supporting an expanded version of the conjecture regarding quantization's role in improving generalization.

Building upon the framework of the classical capacity formula derived from Fannes' inequality and Araki's inequality, this research delves into the quantum extremal surface method, using the latter as a quantum analog to the former. Consequently, the results illuminate capacitary quantum extremal surfaces, which serve as the optimal separators between a specified region and the remainder of a quantum system's spatial domain to minimize the von Neumann entropy of the latter region. Furthermore, the study establishes the quantum counterpart to Grotheruil's theorem and the capacity-additivity formula, demonstrating that the boundary of the spatial domain where these capacitary quantum extremal surfaces reside partitions the quantum system into two disjoint parts, wherein the modular flows of these respective regions' density matrices are entirely contained within their respective regions.

The R-matrix of a solvable lattice model satisfies the Yang-Baxter equation, which contains a parameter influencing both its matrix structure and entry values. The YB equation is an essential relation in a model with a lattice structure, representing the interchange of adjacent interactions, with the 'crossing factor' being a specific element within the R-matrix. The investigation presented here focuses on the 'crossing factor's properties in relation to the Yang-Baxter equation and its impact on lattice model solutions.

This study introduces and evaluates multiple stabilization techniques for iterative algorithms used in compressed sensing, focusing on underdetermined systems with sparsity constraints. Additionally, we investigate the relationship between stabilization methods and extrapolation techniques, while comparing their efficacy through both theoretical analysis and experimental evaluations.

We adopt a comprehensive approach to determine the PSF of a combined image by treating convolution and combination operations as linear transformations. The transformation matrix for combining images is straightforward to compute given the input images, while determining the PSF involves solving a set of linear equations. Although this PSF cannot always be directly calculated due to constraints, it can be efficiently estimated by solving the corresponding normal equations. The resulting estimate along with precise error bounds demonstrates that this method is both a universal solution and the most precise estimator when the PSF estimates are linear. The validity of this estimator in widely used imaging applications, such as image compression and deconvolution, is substantiated by numerical examples. The resulting errors from this normal-equation-based estimator significantly outperform those from the popular psfutil package.

Building upon Edelman and Harris's work and extending it to 2N multiple Schramm-Loewner evolutions and their associated Gaussian free fields in a corner domain, we make a significant modification. We consider these phenomena occurring within a ball instead and demonstrate that the joint distribution of the fields at points inside the ball and on its boundary remains solely determined by the condition that all field values on the boundary are zero.

The Solution to the Navier-Stokes equations can be estimated at its initial stages with respect to the maximum norm of the initial data, which is given in this research paper. The estimation includes the velocity field and its first spatial derivatives, with the solution being valid for periodic initial conditions.

Quantum computation verification is currently a complex and difficult task. A new approach proposed in this paper allows for efficient verification of quantum computations by a potentially untrustworthy quantum device. Notably, this approach is unique in its ability to provide constant query complexity and therefore, linear time verification for any polynomial degree. However, achieving this efficiency comes at the cost of unconditionally changing challenges and consequently, the security level is now dependent on the device's quantum capabilities. To this end, we develop new protocols based on a post-quantum secure outer function and a trusted bit, leveraging qualities such as high min-entropy and negative influence pairs from circuit PCPs. Our proposed verification protocol can handle qubit failures and maintains a trade-off between resource requirements and quantum capabilities. Our work assumes the existence of a trusted bit, a reasonable and minimal requirement that may be met by quantum devices.

This study proposes using implicit neural representations as generated signals, leveraging SVF signed distance functions to model three-dimensional cell structures from 2-dimensional microscopy images. A training dataset of cells, along with their associated MRI scans, enables us to train a neural network that produces complex, hierarchical 3-dimensional cell shapes. The effectiveness of our approach is demonstrated through successful reconstructions and predictions, alongside improvements in other related tasks. Furthermore, we utilize the trained model to create synthetic cell structures and through analysis, identify cell shape characteristics. Lasting contributions are made in several areas, including increased understanding of shape language and its applications in shape completion, shape analysis, and generative modeling of cells.

We initially studied how a simple, local learning rule could model the brain's 3D spatial representation. This space is constructed from sensory inputs in the hippocampus and has a topological structure that allows it to accurately reflect the complexities of the real world. Our analysis reveals that this space's properties enable effective navigation by connecting temporal relationships between an agent's past experiences. Both our results and those of previous studies indicate that the connection between place cells and their sensory inputs is a random structure, which is stable and supports reliable navigation.

To explore complex systems, it is essential to extend our understanding of how our own thoughts and actions interact with our environment. A key aspect of this is our ability to influence and be influenced by our surroundings in a non-symmetrical way. This dynamic is effectively modeled through non-reversible Markov processes. In our research, we have applied non-reversible dynamics to the hard-disk dimer model and found that the system's free energy can be controlled and potentially minimized. Additionally, we've observed that the transport properties of the system, such as the relationship between stress and velocity, vary significantly based on the degree of reversibility. Our study also reveals unique patterns in the local distribution of the system, including the formation of clusters, and we've used our findings to explore the potential for phase transitions as a function of the reversibility parameter.

The challenge of Sound Event Localization and Identification (SELD) lies in pinpointing not only what sound events are occurring but also their directional origins. Recent advances in using rectangular filters and a convolutional neural network known as the crnn have shown promise in this area, however, there is a significant limitation in their field-of-view. To address this issue, a data enhancement strategy called channel rotation is proposed, which involves artificially rotating spatial microphone data to expand the model's field-of-view beyond its original scope. When applied to a dataset called SEAMOD, this approach has demonstrated improved accuracy in identifying sound events not only in the training data but also in unseen directions, outperforming an alternative method that artificially generates additional spatial positions for each microphone.

The growing demand for mobile data and limited wireless spectrum will necessitate innovative technologies to sustain enhanced quality of service. A well-established idea from communication theory suggests that increasing transmission power can improve signal quality. Historically, however, this concept was merely theoretical due to technical limitations. Advances in modern radio electronics enable simultaneous transmission and reception on various frequency bands, turning the traditional paradigm on its head. This results in a significant enhancement in spectral efficiency while using single-antenna hardware. Although initially explored in the context of cellular devices, this paradigm has garnered considerable interest in reward systems that can accurately predict user behavior. This interest is reflected in the increased citations of the paper, reflecting its influence on user check-in dynamics. This paper provides a comprehensive review of ongoing research into the applications and theoretical foundations of concurrent transmission-based wireless systems. A detailed discussion on the underlying principles and architectures of simultaneous transmission hardware is presented, followed by an examination of different learning and control algorithms applicable to these systems. Finally, various solution techniques for simultaneous transmission systems are examined, emphasizing the need for efficient power control to prevent interference, particularly in uplink scenarios. This paper aims to introduce readers to the complexities of simultaneous transmission systems and highlights promising areas of further research.

Time-frequency analysis techniques, such as the Wigner distribution, allow for the examination of signal energy distribution in the time-frequency plane. We propose a new approach for signal detection by analyzing the statistical properties of scale space representations of signals. Energy detecting non-linear transforms will generate a two-dimensional spectrum where energy detectors are plotted as closed curves. The shapes of these curves can be studied using stochastic geometry techniques. The probability distribution of the enclosed areas is derived in this work. An alternative approach for signal examination involves measuring the complexity of the spectrogram level sets using the Hausdorff dimension. We show that this measure can effectively distinguish between a signal and noise with a signal-to-noise ratio of 10 dB. The global structures of the spectrogram level sets provide a framework for feature extraction, offering a novel approach for signal analysis.

The approach involves pinpointing the core aspects of dynamical networks using a combination of dynamical network theory and image processing. Its primary application is the robust detection of coexisting synchronized and unsynchronized regions within a network of oscillators. The methodology effectively tracks the migration of synchronized waves within a network of oscillators that exhibit traveling wave patterns. It provides a user-friendly algorithm that requires only the construction of a dynamical network, making it applicable to various types of oscillatory networks. The methodology has demonstrated successful results in two types of dynamical networks: those composed of Fitzhugh-Nagumo oscillators that exhibit traveling chimeras and those composed of Rossler oscillators that exhibit moving synchronized clusters.

Laplace Demon, a powerful N-body simulation execution framework by Raymond S. Ferrer, excels in simulating complex solar system dynamics. To accurately replicate phenomena like zone transitions, research has increased the number of simulated bodies, necessitating computational efficiency. This research presents a modified script, exc stochastic forces, to mitigate the computational burden of Laplace Demon. The modified script integrates stochastic perturbation simulations into REBOUND, significantly reducing the time required for each time step. Time-dependent numerical tests confirm the code's effectiveness, demonstrating its ability to achieve a substantial reduction in computational time. This modification facilitates Laplace Demon's application on larger planetary ensembles.

An operator equation has been formulated to describe open quantum system dynamics with continuous feedback control, offering a precise mathematical model similar in nature to the Schrodinger equation. This model's integrated numerical method has been employed to simulate the feedback-controlled quantum Gaussian state evolution. Additionally, the effect of feedback control on ground state energy was analyzed in detail.

We've investigated the problem of arranging a collection of blocks of two distinct shapes and masses within a narrow space. The blocks, of different sizes, have a specified number in abundance, and their weights vary based on their form. The goal is to find all possible sequences of blocks that alternate in form, with their weights going up and down in a specific pattern. The block arrangements that follow this pattern are referred to as pseudopermutations. The method of finding these block arrangements involves algorithmic and mathematical methods, and a script has been used to verify the results computationally. The outcome is a new formula block count, which we find equals the Catalan number. The problem's complexity and difficulty make it an intriguing puzzle.

Extreme events of low (drought) and high (flood) precipitation linked to El Ni\~no are strongly influenced by its distinct flavors. We investigate how different flavors of El Ni\~no, specifically Eastern-Pacific and Central-Pacific types, affect global patterns of very low and very high seasonal precipitation. Our analysis reveals that a substantial portion (60-80%) of these events are linked to El Ni\~no, but Eastern- and Central- types have distinct effects on precipitation. Events of low precipitation are mostly associated with Eastern- type, affecting regions in South America, Australia, and Indonesia, while Central- type affects regions in South America, South China, and the Mediterranean Sea. In contrast, both types share similar responses in patterns of very low precipitation in South America. Events of high precipitation are mostly associated with Eastern- and Central- types, affecting regions in Africa and South China respectively, with no dependence on El Ni\~no, but distinct responses in other regions. Our study emphasizes the importance of El Ni\~no, especially its distinct flavors, for understanding and addressing severe drought and flooding, especially in the context of climate change.

To understand massive black hole origins, we need to observe these sub-Newtonian environments in satellite galaxies that haven't merged with their host systems. We studied two dark matter halo satellites orbiting within the Milky Way: Leo I and Segue 1. Leo I exhibits a cluster of stars orbiting at a huge distance, and it's surrounded by sub-Newtonian space due to a dark matter halo. Our star tracker found multiple stars potentially orbiting the supermassive black hole in Leo I, with one path potentially leading to a sub-Newtonian region. This could create a unique environment where black hole-fed stars explode due to accreting gas from cloud passages, leaving behind star clusters like the one we see in Leo I.

In this study, we investigate the impact of electron correlations on the low-temperature magnetic properties of a Kagome lattice, using the Cr-doped NiS$_{2-x}$Se$_{2+x}$ system. Through our DFT and DMFT calculations, we demonstrate that Krönig-Moore-type flat bands in the Kagome lattice give rise to strong electron correlations. These flat bands contribute towards localized states below the Fermi level, whose position can be adjusted by changing the Cr concentration and thus a magnetic gap forms. This results in negative magnetoresistance at low-temperature, which we attribute to the interplay between the flat bands and strong electron correlations. Our alloy study, that combines the ab-initio and DMFT methods effectively, reveals the mechanism behind the observation of negative magnetoresistance in materials with flat bands.

By analyzing functional annotation of genomic regions identified in genome-wide association studies, researchers discovered that a substantial portion of associated variants play a role in gene regulation rather than coding sequences. This study re-evaluates the utility of various functional annotations by jointly considering multiple stategies, addressing common pitfalls and comparing the functional relevance of associated, neutral, and randomly selected variants. 

In the process of re-assessing the quality of functional annotations, re-evaluates the utility of examining gene regulation patterns in neutral regions, re-emphasizes the importance of analyzing chromatin accessibility rather than just the orientation of annotations, and confirms that substantial associations with expression levels are found in neutral regions. 

In addition to re-evaluating the utility of functional annotations, this study re-emphasizes the importance of considering multiple functional annotations in association studies and points out that many reports of association with gene expression may be misleading due to inappropriate statistical methods. 

Re-evaluates the utility of functional annotations in association studies of 18 human traits, providing re-calculations of results in major studies in this field.

This study classifies all finite groups that permit multiple transitivity over a set of size $q^r$, where the prime number $r$ and a number $\lambda$ are relatively prime. Specifically, it has been established that such a group either allows for a unique orbit of size $r+1$ or can be broken down into a specific type of product group structure.

The effectiveness of entropy-based criteria in evaluating wave functions for quantum systems was examined. This evaluation took place for helium-like atoms in various confinement conditions. Specifically, entropies were calculated using the Fisher information for electron density and the joint electron density. Entropy components and behavior were also named, and their relationship with correlation was found to be asymptotically proportional. It was found that entropy criteria effectively account for correlation effects in these confined systems, even in the presence of significant one-electron kinetic energy. Moreover, it was observed that entropy criteria were particularly useful for evaluating wave functions where Coulomb correlation plays a dominant role, rather than kinetic energy.

The gravity test is usually performed through observations of planetary motions within the solar system, but by measuring stellar distances using laser interferometry, the same process can be conducted with potentially greater precision. The sample of wide binary stars is sufficiently large to yield valuable results. Specifically, the cross correlation between HST and Gaia star positions has provided an alternative assessment, indicating that Newton's inverse square law is consistent with observations, with an error margin of approximately 35 kilometers per second squared. Furthermore, no detectable influence of the jordanian-euro metric is observed within the same constraints.
To multiplicative linear logic without units, The multiplicative dual-intermediate theorem is applied, extended with the logic's multiplicative negation concept.

Financial time series synchronization is crucial for synchronized trading strategies, 
however, measuring it is a complex task. Traditional methods like correlation or coherence 
can assess linear connections or frequency-based connections, but they fall short in capturing dynamic or non-linear relationships. 
Predicting synchronous trends ahead of time is essential for creating reliable synchronization indicators. 
This study introduces an advanced method for analysis and prediction of synchronization 
in financial time series. It involves using time-delayed embedding to construct a three-dimensional phase space, 
calculating cross-recurrence plots (CRPs) to represent dynamics, and converting the cross-recurrence rate and typical time 
derived from the CRPs into feature vectors for machine learning. 
For feature selection, it utilizes random forest and evaluates the proposed method's effectiveness 
using predictions on stock market data.

A model that incorporates the effects of phonon emission, absorption, and dispersion is developed, focusing on the influence of momentum on phonon interactions. It's shown that phonon emission and absorption are not symmetric processes due to the gain from the phonon source term being greater than the loss from the spreading term. Moreover, spin-flipping, phonon coupling does not conform to conventional ideas. Instead, it generates a complex, off-diagonal effect represented by the spin-orbit force, which acts as a source of in-plane spin density current despite conserving the total spin. Finally, it is possible that a momentum-dependent phonon interaction results in a shift from the spin-optical phonon mediated Rashba effect to a more conventional spin-phonon coupling scenario.

Advertisements with new images face a challenge known as the "cold start" issue, which limits their ability to attract users and collect data due to their limited exposure. This problem is compounded by the difficulty in utilizing interaction data, as ads without user interactions cannot be trained. Researchers have attempted to address this issue, but no single solution has been effective. This paper introduces a novel approach, which combines visual content analysis with user behavior models to overcome the shortcoming. Specifically, the researchers develop a model that uses visual information to make predictions in place of interaction data where available, and combines this with a pre-trained image model to further improve accuracy. This model's performance outpaces existing methods on the widely used Broad CTR dataset.

The Software Composition Framework leverages design patterns, encoded as language modules, to construct complex software systems. We view these design patterns as a language, defining terms as questions and modules as answers. To formulate precise inquiries, we introduce the design pattern investigation framework, built upon an extension of Maude's HATS with maude-rp, allowing for the integration of constraints and maintenance of design pattern states. We propose the use of case models, offering meta-level perspectives on design pattern investigations, and outline methods for generating them from existing investigation modules. Furthermore, a special type of case model, known as knowledge base, facilitates the organization and management of investigation components.

Wildfires are intensifying in frequency and intensity due to climate change, generating significant thermal radiation and hazardous optical effects that threaten human health and aviation safety. Wild fire analysis poses a significant challenge in remote sensing due to rapid flare development and the limited temporal resolution of satellites. Therefore, continuous and reliable wild fire monitoring requires high spatial and temporal resolution data from multiple sources. While multi-spectral visible light satellites like MODIS, VIIRS, and Sentinel-2 have a lower temporal resolution, they have lower error rates than infrared satellites like OMI, GOES, ARGOS, ASTER, and Landsat-8. Conversely, thermal and infrared satellites, although having a lower error rate, have a lower temporal resolution. Therefore, accurate and real-time wildfire monitoring requires combining multiple data sources. Wildfire analysis has a complex and non-stationary nature, making it unsuitable for traditional methods. Therefore, real-time and reliable wildfire monitoring has become a critical issue. Wildfire analysis using multi-spectral and thermal/infrared data has been shown to provide a lower or higher rate of errors respectively. Therefore, accurate and real-time wildfire monitoring has become a critical issue. Wildfire monitoring has been shown to be a dynamic process that does not conform to conventional satellite remote sensing. The utility of location tracking data is significantly impacted by privacy concerns, specifically those related to identifying specific individuals based on their travel patterns. Traditional differentials, such as the Rényi differential, fall short in addressing tracking privacy issues since they primarily focus on the proximity between data points rather than their distance. To effectively measure tracking privacy, we introduce the concept of tracking differentials, which compare the distances between corresponding paths of distributions defined on spatial locations, rather than just their distributions. Building upon this foundation, we propose a new framework for evaluating tracking privacy that incorporates conditional priors. This framework recognizes that at each timestamp, a user's location distribution is partially dependent on their historical location. Furthermore, we introduce the tracking $f$-differential, a generalization of the $f$-differential that incorporates conditional priors. We apply this concept to popular functions $f$, such as the Kullback-Leibler, Itô, and Helming divergences, and demonstrate its practical value through a case study of the Google Maps locator.

Research on resting-state functional MRI (rs-fMRI) has been influenced by evidence suggesting that active brain networks can be detected through dynamic signal correlations. However, the reliability of this approach has not been thoroughly evaluated using rigorous statistical methods. In response to this gap, we developed a novel framework combining simulation, prediction analysis, and anomaly detection anomalies to assess the reliability and predictive capability of rs-fMRI data. By applying advanced statistical techniques such as generalized linear models (GLMs) along with regularisation methods like minimal l1-plus-l2 regularization (MILAR) and elastic net (EN), we demonstrated that new methods can yield superior performance in predicting external variables and that precise prediction timelines can be established. In particular, we found that RS-fMRI data could accurately predict heart rate variability with an R2 value of 0.41 and that brain regions associated with this prediction formed distinct networks. Additionally, we discovered significant connections between rs-fMRI prediction R2 values and individual variations, such as age, attention deficits, anxiety levels, and head movement. Notably, we identified a network centered around the anterior cingulate-prefrontal cortex that overlaps with default mode network regions and has been previously linked to vegetative states and attention deficits. These results provide a foundation for validating rs-fMRI's utility in understanding individual brain function, identifying personal variation patterns, and potentially identifying early signs of health disorders.

Building upon previous work, we combine estimates of heat semigroups with gradient bounds to demonstrate the existence of a concentration phenomenon for directed graphs that adhere to a lower bound on Ricci curvature. This result generalizes a phenomenon observed in structures with symmetric relationships, and we also derive a estimate for the logarithmic Sobolev inequality in this context.

Recent advancements in Natural Language Processing have seen a significant surge in multilingual capabilities, which have been largely absent for Indian language pairs due to a lack of resources, particularly for low-resource Indian code-mixed languages. This paper addresses the limitation by developing PESTO, a positional encoding framework tailored for small datasets of Indian code-mixed languages. Moreover, our research introduces innovative techniques to address the challenges associated with place- and region-specific name categories. Experimental results indicate that PESTO achieves superior performance on the Indian code-mixed dataset when paired with transformers. Additionally, our findings suggest that PESTO exhibits promising potential for improving the training efficiency of transformers on data-sparse Indian code-mixed datasets.

The high-temperature superconductivity of certain materials like iron pnictides and transition metal dichalcogenides has been found to share a common electronic characteristic known as the van Hove singularity (VHS). This feature has also been present in theoretical models of MgB$_2$ and, most notably, in the high-temperature superconductor H$_3$TS under pressure. We have found that the resistance of H$_3$TS to optimization using VHS is weak, and this resistance is similar to that observed in MgB$_2$. Moreover, the maximum critical temperature of around 255 K for MgB$_2$ is achieved at a specific doping level that corresponds to the VHS being at the Fermi level, and this VHS-driven resistance has been supported by density functional theory and many-body simulations for H$_3$TS, where it predicts a specific value of the effective electron-phonon coupling constant, $\lambda_{\text{eff}}$, which is similar to that found in MgB$_2$.

A number of scholars have shown that post-selection events are not inherently correlated with pre-selection events, citing Fisher's (1930) concept of the average effect, which they have later applied to (Fisher, 1930; Hallman and Schulte, 2015; Schulte, 2015; Schurz andauer, 2015; Schurz, 2016; Schurz, 2017; Schurz, 2018; Schurz, 2019; Schurz, 2020; Schurz, 2021). To address concerns raised by critics such as Hallman and Schulte (2015) and Schulte (2015), who argued that Fisher's finding and subsequent generalization do not adequately demonstrate the non-causal nature of the selection process, we present an explanation of why it is crucial that the selection process does not cause it, and demonstrate how average effect and its generalized form satisfy this requirement.

Achieving robust and efficient bipedal locomotion remains a significant challenge, 
with bipedal robots typically relying on alternating support legs without external support. 
This has been a limitation that many successful humanoid robots encounter, 
with the exception of quadrupeds, which easily utilize two support legs for thrust. 
To overcome this, researchers explore the use of on-demand thrusters for supplemental 
external support in addition to existing bipedal robots, 
resulting in a novel model that integrates bipedal dynamics with optional thrust forces. 
This integrated model, when compared to traditional methods, has shown robust performance 
in simulation and real-world testing, with a required energy reduction of up to 60%.

This research proposes a visual relocalization technique based on geometric information derived from 3D surfel mapping. A comprehensive database of keyframes, created with 3D semantic segmentation, enables efficient global matching of query images. While prior studies have explored using semantic labels to enhance relocalization, this work investigates learning image descriptors that incorporate these labels to facilitate global matching. Additionally, since keyframe extraction is critical to relocalization performance, this study proposes an attention-based method based on neural radiance fields that improves the effectiveness of coarse 3D surfel mapping. By integrating surface normals and semantic information, this attention-based approach achieves superior accuracy in relocalization compared to standard methods.

Deciding a neural network's untrained layers remains an unresolved issue in deep learning.
In the context of Federated Semi-Supervised Learning (FSSL), employing semi-
supervised learning algorithms exacerbates the problem due to the varying choices of
deeper untrained layers across devices despite them having trained on distinct data.
To resolve this, FSSL algorithms must minimize ambiguity for optimal performance.
However, minimizing ambiguity for FSSL presents a new challenge. 
Our research introduces a novel strategy to resolve this issue by using the CoVarEntropy measure, which integrates variability minimization and entropy minimization.
We integrate this strategy with a current FSSL technique and evaluate its efficacy on multiple datasets. 
The outcomes show that our approach surpasses existing methods on certain datasets.

Simulations of second-long black hole-neutron star mergers in numerical relativity have been performed to obtain a comprehensive picture of the radiation-powered jet emission. The study focuses on how various factors, including the spin of the neutron star, the strength and structure of the magnetic field, and the neutron star's equation of state, affect results. The findings of earlier, short-duration simulations have been expanded to reveal the long-term behavior of these events and the impact of a neutron star with lower stiffness on jet dynamics. Notably, such collisions can produce powerful electromagnetic bursts lasting several seconds even without the presence of a field-aligned jet mechanism. However, the intensity of these bursts is highly sensitive to the neutron star's magnetic structure, with peak power reaching up to $10^{52}$ erg s$^{-1}$ during the early post merger phase. If the neutron star contains substantial stored magnetic energy, this can be channeled into the jet, resulting in extended, intense emission at frequencies typical of gamma-ray bursts. The research indicates that initial conditions and equations of state play a pivotal role in shaping the dynamics and radiation of these black hole-neutron star collisions over several seconds.

For a compact Riemann surface of genus $g\geq 2$ with a constant negative curvature metric, we introduce a core attribute, $L$, which depends on its associated Hilbert space. This attribute, $L$, can be expressed as the sum of $(2g+1-\delta)$ squared terms representing the first eigenvalue, $\lambda_1$, plus twice the sum of all subsequent discrete eigenvalues, which results in a finite quantity. We demonstrate that the attribute $L$ is bounded from below by a function of $\mathrm{area}(X)$, that converges to zero as the area tends to infinity, by examining the case where the infimum is achieved, where it is possible to establish a rigorous lower bound for the attribute $L$; in addition to this we will construct instances in which $L$ approaches zero as the area tends to infinity via a rigorous mathematical proof that verifies the convergence rate for surfaces that have a symmetry.

We establish a novel method to establish non-asymptotic upper bounds for the deviation of the cumulative distribution function of standard normal distribution from the Q-function across the entire real line, featuring a unique expression for the approximation error.

This research explores the optical interaction between a light source and two nanoparticles near a graphene sheet. By positioning the nanoparticles in close proximity, coupling between their plasmons is induced through the graphene plasma. Specifically, the authors investigate how this positioning affects the resonance frequencies of the plasmons within the graphene sheet. Based on theoretical calculations, the studies reveal that the plasmons can be bound to the dimer or free-space resonances can be made non-radiative. A notable finding is that the terahertz range is particularly sensitive to changes in the graphene chemical potential, enabling efficient coupling between light and matter at this frequency.

In an emergency department, the length of a patient's stay is influenced by how many patients are being treated at the same time, leading to delays in treatment for subsequent patients. The duration of patients who arrive after the peak time, whose numbers are decreasing, is affected by a different factor: the type of patients triaged as more serious is usually longer. The duration of EC patients, regardless of arrival time, is also impacted by other issues, such as the availability of medical resources like examination rooms and the timely arrival of lab results. The simultaneous occurrence of these factors means that the duration of EC patients, on average, is affected by a combination of congestion and disease severity, at different times and when medical resources are being used efficiently.

In this research, we investigate the strategic interaction between two groups of robots performing multiple synchronized tasks on a graph. Each group decides on its task order and scheduling, considering factors such as limited communication and processing capabilities, graph constraints, and communication delays. Both groups aim to maximize their respective throughputs by selecting optimal task sequences and scheduling strategies. This paper establishes an existence proof for Nash equilibria in this scenario, which we demonstrate through experimental results obtained from simulated robot simulations.

A study examining the potential impact of chiral magnetic influence in high-energy particle collisions involved calculating azimuthal angle correlations between charged particles. Calculations were based on particle momentum and charge, a method known as the four-vector balance parameter $B_4$. Analysis involved selecting events from the ALICE collaboration, which occurred at high-energy levels of 2.76 and 5.02 TeV in Pb-Pb collisions. Measurements were taken across varying collision centrality, and comparisons with theoretical predictions using the AMoCA model, which amasses contributions from multiple sources. However, analysis suggests that the potential chiral magnetic influence accounts for less than 0.5% of the total azimuthal angle correlations.

The rapid growth of the crowdfunding market presents both a potential solution and a challenge, as it allows fundraisers to crowdsource validation for their projects while also encountering an overwhelming number of projects competing for funding, leading to extremely low success rates. In response to this challenge, researchers seek to understand what types of crowd-generated signals can help distinguish between failing and succeeding fundraising campaigns. Through a multi-platform study spanning 2015-2019 on the scales of millions and tens of millions, respectively, the authors examined crowd-sourced activity on Kickstarter and GoFundMe related to fundraising project/foundation attributes, interactions, and content. The analysis revealed key crowd signals associated with fundraising campaigns that ultimately succeed, such as interaction between fundraisers and the public, and the level of engagement with these platforms. Notably, the authors found that the public's meaningful involvement in a project or cause can be a stronger predictor of fundraising success than the campaign itself. Moreover, differences in fundraising success were observed between the two platforms, with specific attributes and crowd-generated signals being more valuable in succeeding on each. These findings provide insights into the types of projects and causes that can effectively utilize crowdfunding, such as those that actively interact with the public and have strong levels of engagement.

The application of machine learning to network intrusion detection has been utilized by researchers and practitioners for over a decade. Notably, major security firms rely on this method to safeguard their customers. A significant drawback of this method is that it discards valuable data upon detection of a network intrusion by submitting all data to a remote server, which limits the ability to discover new attacks and keeps users isolated within separate security domains. To address this limitation, this paper proposes an innovative approach where a federated learning algorithm is implemented for network intrusion detection to prevent data loss and retain security information on local devices. The benefits of federated learning are explored in this paper, which shows how it facilitates the exchange of knowledge among security domains and increases overall security. The applicability of federated learning for classification and detection tasks is explored, which is crucial for cyber threat intelligence sharing in the context of network intrusion detection.

Recent advancements in logistics automation have led to the adoption of multi-robot systems, significantly enhancing handling efficiency. A critical issue in multi-robot logistics is to optimize task sequencing to minimize travel distances. While literature exists on multi-robot path planning, it often overlooks the impact of task ordering. Our research addresses this gap, focusing on a scenario involving four robots with distinct starting positions and a task set comprising four targets, each assigned to a specific robot. We establish an upper bound for the optimal solution and propose an efficient grouping algorithm, demonstrating its polynomial-time complexity and validity. Under specific conditions, our results indicate the proposed approach yields a task sequence within 50% of the optimal solution. We further develop two strategies to refine the bounds, showing significant improvements over existing methods. Our experiments utilize real data from an automated warehouse setting, showcasing the practical feasibility and performance of our approach.

The suitability of CMOS technology for device modeling and analysis is well-documented, but the precise measurement of transfer length has limited its use for this purpose. By employing full band structure calculations, quantum mechanical tunneling, and 3D finite element methods within a full 300mm CMOS process, we have derived an equation to calculate the transfer length. This enables a transfer length analysis of SiMOSFETs, resulting in the design of devices with exceptionally high mobility.

Accurate exchange of information between branches in an academic field relies on effective communication and mutual understanding. The question arises as to how knowledge is successfully transmitted and how expertise develops within a field over time. To answer these questions, we used numerical simulations to model an hypothetical field with multiple groups and a public database. The initial public knowledge was distributed unevenly among groups, and only publicly shared individual contributions added to the public knowledge pool. Our study revealed that, despite starting conditions, each group tends to master a specific problem-solving approach. The public knowledge composition becomes diverse, and overall progress slows down, unless there is consistent knowledge sharing within each group. Our findings imply that maintaining balanced group knowledge is essential for rapid public advancement in rapidly evolving fields.

Our research focuses on improving video search result quality by addressing the issue of source variety bias. This problem stems from the over-reliance on a limited range of video sources, which can cause users to miss out on high-quality videos from diverse creators. This study investigates the source composition of top video search results from leading platforms, revealing a significant bias towards a small proportion of providers. To mitigate this issue, we have developed an approach that identifies and addresses the source variety bias in video search outcomes. Our method involves integrating a real-time virtual agent, similar to those found on popular video sharing sites, which can assess the quality and diversity of each video's provider. This approach allows the system to identify and prioritize videos from reputable sources, thereby improving the relevance and fairness of search results. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method through automated assessments and user testing, showing a noticeable increase in the diversity of video sources and a corresponding boost in user engagement and satisfaction.

In our investigation of four-dimensional N=1 Wess-Zumino models using the bootstrap method, we identified a distinctive feature - a gradual decline in specific numerical markers associated with primary operators as they increase in scaling dimensions. This pattern appears to be heavily influenced by a limited set of higher-spin primary operators and their associated currents. The monodromy anomaly arising from this pattern poses significant hurdles to systematically advancing the bootstrap analysis through the inclusion of increasingly distant contributions. Notably, the magnitude of this phenomenon cannot be accounted for by the contributions of lower-spin currents alone. Within the context of known solutions, the three-point interactions involving the leading spin-3/2 current appear to be the main source responsible for this anomaly. Furthermore, the anomaly can also be traced back to the contributions of higher-spin primary operators present in the spectrum. Crucially, the standard extrapolation methods when applied to this system yield incorrect results, including non-unitary values for coupling constants. A simplified approach, in which the monodromy effect is minimized, leads to a more realistic unitary solution.

We establish the existence of an elliptic curve over a cubic field extension with a non-reducible definition, featuring a point on its graph with a level of 13. This is achieved through the utilization of modular degrees and bounds associated with elliptic curves over quadratic fields, specifically those introduced by Greenberg and Strauss. Furthermore, we identify numerous other instances of elliptic curves over such fields with points at a level of 13, as well as an elliptic curve with a point at a level of 7, accompanied by corresponding ranks.

In unlicensed frequency bands, wireless devices often experience significant interference due to various devices operating simultaneously without coordination. Current high-speed wireless technologies, which rely on medium access methods such as frequency division multiple access and code division multiple access, effectively handle and eliminate inter-device interference. This paper examines the possibility of achieving similar results using random access methods. Specifically, the authors propose a interference handling method based on interference cancellation, interference averaging, or interference suppression suitable for random access protocols. The paper then assesses the feasibility of employing interference management techniques compatible with existing high-speed wireless standards and suggests solutions for integrating them into random access systems. A notable finding of the paper is the significant potential of utilizing interference management to improve the performance of random access systems through interference averaging.

When working with few labels, a common strategy involves utilizing pseudo-tags created from self or semi-supervised learning. These pseudo-tags enable the unlabelled data to contribute to the training process. However, the effectiveness of pseudo-tags heavily depends on their quality, and often they can be inaccurate due to the limitations of self-supervised and semi-supervised learning algorithms. These methods typically focus on preserving the data's structural characteristics, rather than tag accuracy. To overcome this issue, we have created a graph pseudo-tagting approach called Informative Pseudo-Tagging (IPT), which improves both the overall and specific outcomes. The IPT method identifies unlabelled data with accurate pseudo-tags and discards the rest, allowing only the useful data to be included in the training process. The utility of an data point is determined by the similarity of its pseudo-tag to the available labels and its connectivity to the data with available labels in the graph. The results show that using pseudo-tags without filtering significantly hampers performance compared to not employing them at all. Conversely, using filter pseudo-tags (IPT) improves overall performance and precision, recall, F1 score, and AUC compared to a system without pseudo-tags.

We propose an efficient short-range pattern matching network, called PatchNet, for
extracting low-frequency, large-scale structural information in videos. Given the
high computational cost associated with conventional full-frame processing methods,
our approach divides each frame into multiple smaller patches, applies neural networks
independently to extract structural info, and consolidates the results. This breaks
the dependency between low and high-frequency components, enabling the efficient
processing of videos. We evaluate the performance of our approach on several
benchmark video enhancement and low-light video enhancement datasets. Furthermore,
we develop an end-to-end end-to-end pipeline, integrating patch-based short-range
structural extraction with other strategies, and demonstrate its potential on
basic video up-sampling and low-light conditions. The code supporting this work
can be accessed at the following link: https://github.com/Fei-AG/VideoPatchNet

We examine the time evolution of the discrete-time Kuperberg-truncated asymmetric simple exclusion process on a 1D lattice with periodic boundaries. Leveraging recent findings from Johnson, O'Rourke, and Remenik regarding multi-time distributions in the continuous-time asymmetric exclusion process, we determine the exact distribution of particle positions at multiple time instances for the discrete system with a finite number of particles. This yields a major discrete/continuous time equivalence and leads to new known and novel results. Notably, we obtain closed-form expressions for the joint distributions of particle positions at multiple time instances, which were unpreviously known in the continuous-time model.

A new wireless communication strategy, known as wireless information power transfer (WIPT), has gained attention due to its potential for integrating power harvesting and battery charging. To address the limitations of energy-constrained devices, we investigate an efficient system design in which a base station transmits using a fixed scheme that supports multiple services, including SWIPT, in a mobile wireless network. We explore an optimal way to distribute a base station's transmit power across different frequencies in order to maximize the overall energy efficiency. Furthermore, we develop a dynamic scheduling technique based on queueing theory to ensure that the base station operates at a stable and fair rate. Simulation results demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed approach compared to existing schemes.

In the limit where the number of components N is infinite for p-wave interaction, we develop a theoretical framework, resulting in an infinite-N theory that we apply to analyze SU(M) interactions (where N and M are odd integers). This analysis shows that the structure of infinite-N p-wave interactions is governed by two key parameters: one controls p-wave scattering while the other influences p-wave interaction between different spin states. We apply this framework to SU(N) interactions where the number of components N is 3,5, and 7. A detailed analysis of the effective p-wave scattering and p-wave interaction is provided, and a systematic expansion in 1/N is formulated, and is found to expand around an infinite-N p-wave scattering energy level. Furthermore, we examine the properties of quasisparticles at infinite-N p-wave scattering energy in detail. When p-wave interaction between different spin states becomes extremely strong, it leads to spontaneous symmetry breaking, and our analysis shows this occurs at specific p-wave coupling strengths for each spin configuration. Analytical calculations of critical p-wave coupling strengths are performed, and are complemented by numerical calculations, and it is found that 1/N expansion provides accurate results. While 1/N expansion offers reliable results for p-wave scattering energy and critical p-wave coupling strength, it fails when attempting to calculate other physical properties like p-wave scattering cross-section. Therefore, while 1/N expansion is a valuable tool for understanding infinite-N p-wave properties, additional corrections are necessary for a comprehensive

In optomechanical systems, the interaction between light and motion can be effectively modeled using a classical approach. This involves equating the optical cavity with an electric resonator and representing mechanical vibrations as a mass-spring system. Since this classical description excludes thermal effects, we propose a semi-classical model inspired by the Einstein-Smolensky mass-spring system. This new model incorporates a noise current that emulates the influence of thermal fluctuations. Both the quantum optomechanical and the quantum-electro-elastic (QEE) models are shown through their respective circuit diagrams in Figure 1.

The study focuses on orthogonal polynomials connected to a matrix derived from a parameterized trigonometric polynomial, and a method is proposed for analyzing zeros of generalized Airy polynomials in any dimension. This method employs the theory of linear difference equations, leading to the conclusion that the proposed derivation reduces to the classical Airy case when the dimension is one. The study's findings originate from the theory of line bundles and sections within a vector bundle, specifically the L^2-sections.

This study examines the behavioral patterns of a robot that adheres to walls, focusing on the impact of sensor inaccuracies. Through numerical simulations, researchers discovered that the robot's trajectory can either settle into a stable state, break into a repetitive cycle, or result in wall-colliding outcomes. By mapping out the probability of colliding with a wall, they identified multiple zones of varying stability and found that the robot's ability to avoid collisions sometimes transitions abruptly between these zones. These results align with an analytical model, and the finding that small errors in parameters can shift from coexisting stable limits suggests a complex relationship between the robot's control systems and its ability to navigate successfully.

Building on earlier developments within the framework of algebraic QFT in 2 dimensions, we have further refined it by incorporating algebraic techniques to analyze fermionic theories with chiral symmetry. This involves constructing a universal algebra, which serves as the foundation for all such theories. We have specifically applied these principles to the free complex fermion theory, and have examined its propagator and the structure of its space of solutions. Moreover, we have explored the technique of chiral switching within this context.

Laparoscopic surgery relies on a camera that captures visible light to capture internal body parts and any present smoke from electrosurgery. Developments in image enhancement algorithms have been primarily focused on improving the quality of images, though their effectiveness in identifying smoke has yet to be explored. This study investigates whether image enhancement techniques can facilitate the detection of smoke, with experimental results showing that enhancing visible light images does not always lead to improved smoke visibility. Variations in smoke properties, such as density, thickness, and surface texture, play a significant role in their visibility, suggesting that smoke's optical characteristics are key to its visibility. Consequently, when shifting from detecting original to enhanced images, semantic segmentation algorithms require retraining. Based on our findings, it is recommended that semantic segmentation algorithms be trained directly on raw, unmodified images.

Researchers investigate the development of deterministic quantum logic operations using the Molmer-Sorensen gate technique in a chain of ions. They analyze the effects of fluctuations in ion frequency on operational stability and successfully achieve compensation of these effects through careful selection of ion motion frequencies, allowing for frequency averaging and thus enhancing performance in mixed-crystal systems with diverse ion properties.

The establishment of a novel structural prototype theory for complex lattices has facilitated the comprehensive, systematic, and theoretical prediction of a vast range of materials. This is particularly relevant to the study of titanium-dated barium atoms. Although within a certain temperature range, the atoms' arrangement is stable, beyond this point, it transforms into a stable, symmetric phase. Calculations by researchers indicate that a wide range of similar materials also display a distinct, highly symmetric phase, and an unusual, disordered phase, and when in this state, materials are unlikely to become stable. This is supported by the researchers finding that a wide range of materials' atoms' arrangement is similar to that of materials with a wide range of other, distinct atomic arrangements.

Two types of infinite dimensional random vectors can be represented as functions over specific domains. The composition of these vectors follows specific rules: the elemental parts are continuous random variables for the first vector type and continuous for the second. The behavior and relationships between these elements are characterized by their respective covariance functions. When analyzing combinations of these vectors, Functional Gaussian Graphical Models and Graphical Gaussian Processes are employed. These models are useful in understanding patterns in various data sets, such as brain activity, protein structures, and blood flow. However, there has been a lack of connection established between these two models. This article fills this knowledge gap by exploring the connection between these models, comparing their strengths and applications, and providing a unified framework for model development.

Quantum state preparation aims to prepare a target quantum state from a simple starting state. Various quantum circuit algorithms aim to achieve this goal, often resulting in complex target states characterized by statistical properties rather than specific values. This state preparation problem contains recurring patterns in its solutions, which can be leveraged to design more efficient and streamlined quantum circuits. A novel method is introduced, which is based on the concept of Markov chains, to automatically compile these circuits. It involves transforming a probability distribution into a quantum state, which is accomplished by iteratively applying a transition matrix (Markov chain) that encapsulates a unitary circuit. This approach enables the compilation of quantum circuits de novo, as well as a more resource-efficient implementation of the algorithm by Phair et al. at random quantum circuit state preparation. Notably, the proposed method successfully replicates the output probability distributions of both approaches. A key benefit of this approach is its ability to model a N-isotope Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution with significantly fewer qubits and gates, specifically N (qubits) and (gates), which outperforms existing methods that require 2N (qubits) and (gates).

We investigate the reliability of average outcomes in a wide array of problems, all of which rely on specific transformation methods. These problems, including a broad range of machine learning and optimization tasks, are characterized by specific mathematical properties. Our analysis reveals that specific tail behaviors in the distribution of evaluation metrics can significantly affect the reliability of average predictions. Additionally, certain robust optimization methods exhibit low sensitivity to disturbances, both of which imply the importance of tail behaviors. These findings provide insights into achieving reliable solutions through optimization techniques.

We examine the low-energy electronic structures of a two-layer system, where interlayer interactions lead to the formation of an excitonic insulating ground state, by means of world-line quantum Monte Carlo methods. To investigate this phenomenon, we develop a numerical technique combining the approach of majorization-type auxiliary field with the local spectral function analysis method. Our results show that distinct peaks in the spectral functions correspond to three types of excitations within the excitonic insulator: bound electron-hole pairs within each layer, and charged excitons having lost an electron or gained one. These spectral features serve as a foundation for proposing a novel application of angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy to study this type of insulator. In particular, we suggest that the auxiliary peaks could offer valuable insights into exciting a superfluid state from a normal state through assisting the removal of an electron or a hole from pairs of electrons and holes.

Our network's unique design allows it to operate without ground truth assumptions on radio signals, enabling more accurate localization. The significant discrepancies between modeled and measured signals, often referred to as signal discrepancies, are the primary challenge. Since these discrepancies are influenced by ground reflections and building irregularities, they are highly variable and difficult to account for. Conventional adaptive padding algorithms, which are widely used in localizations, rely heavily on ground truth assumptions and are therefore unsuitable for this context. To overcome this limitation, we have developed a new message transmission-based adaptive padding algorithm that eliminates the need for ground truth assumptions. Additionally, we have designed an iterative message transmission network to minimize errors and improve tracking. Unlike other error correction algorithms that are only valid under specific linear conditions, our message transmission network is universally applicable. To validate the effectiveness of the algorithm, we have conducted experiments in a real-world setting and the results show significant error reduction.

The interaction patterns of $W$ and $Z$ bosons are studied in proton-proton collisions. Analyzing a vast dataset collected by the ATLAS detector at a 13 TeV proton collision energy, researchers measured joint polarization behaviors of $W$ and $Z$ bosons. These measurements were quantified using angular distribution correlations of decay products of $W$ and $Z$ bosons. Researchers found that certain theoretical models accurately align with experimental data, and discrepancies between measurements and theoretical predictions were within statistical margins of approximately 1.2 standard deviations for joint polarization states of $W$ and $Z$ bosons. These joint polarization state measurements were derived from a sample of $W$ and $Z$ boson events, and separate investigations of individual $Z$ and $W$ boson properties revealed discrepancies that are within about 1.2 standard deviations from theoretical predictions. These measurements primarily affected calculations of relative spin projection coefficients and were found to be consistent with theoretical predictions. Notably, differences between measurements and theoretical predictions were found to affect the $Z$ boson longitudinal polarization fraction ($f_L$") and were found to be around 0.03 above the standard model predictions.

We developed a method to express the Weyl tensor in terms of the Ricci rotation coefficients and explored its implications under the flat spacetime constraint, demonstrating that the Weyl tensor must vanish. This led us to interpret individual terms as quantifiable gravitational effects, thereby creating the Fabric tensor. Our method relies on the Newman-Penrose formalism and offers a clear, computational framework for representing the Weyl tensor, allowing us to interpret its decomposition into NP coefficients as a detailed representation of gravitational wave dynamics.

Researchers explored the connection between orthomodular lattices and their corresponding spatial structures known as Smith stones. They then established a lattice-specific notion of topological duality, pairing an orthomodular lattice with its Smith stone, and proved the existence of a topological duality within this framework.

We introduce a visual representation system that translates Coq proof scripts into an easier-to-process form. Our visual representation uses a set of graphical elements to concisely capture the essence and structure of the original proof script. Building on this foundation, we develop a visual proof inspection tool that is built with D3.js and renders these graphical elements in a web-based interface. The tool allows users to navigate through their Coq proofs in an interactive, visual manner, thereby enhancing proof management capabilities.

For a specific type of mathematical object known as holomorphic Hecke cusp forms, we have determined the limit of the fourth moment over the form with the highest weight in a given range. This study refines a previous finding by Soundararajan in a particular aspect. The ultimate goal is to upgrade Soundarararajan's result to be comparable to what Soundararajan achieved in his work on the extended Riemann zeta function, and evaluate the relevance of the obtained outcome for investigating the L-function associated with automorphic forms.

This paper introduces an innovative method for determining the solution accuracy of linear systems solved by iterative algorithms known as Krylov solvers. Specifically, we focus on a system of linear equations arising from the interior point method for solving optimization problems. Since interior point methods widely utilize Krylov solvers to solve this system, accurately assessing their convergence is crucial. We utilize a vector sequence generated by the predictor-corrector interior point method to create a novel criterion for stopping Krylov solvers. This criterion effectively balances the costs associated with premature and late stopping, as validated through numerical experiments.
