We have developed a low-cost, efficient method for semantic segmentation using hyperspectral images. This approach takes advantage of the numerous channels in hyperspectral images to compensate for the lack of detailed semantic information, which can be achieved without extensive fine-tuning even with limited data available. The cost of hyperspectral images is significantly lower than that of RGB images, which enables us to leverage a pre-trained model that has been adapted to interpret spectral data. By using a large dataset with rich spectral information to train the model and adapting it to process spectral data efficiently, we can effectively utilize the available information in hyperspectral images for semantic segmentation tasks. Our method has been demonstrated to work on a dataset of hyperspectral images in the urban environment and has shown to be an affordable solution for semantic segmentation.

A white dwarf's recent interaction with a giant gas planet has left astronomers wondering. Instead of rotating slowly as expected, the star is spinning at an unexpectedly high speed. The interaction occurred about 300 million years ago, well after angular momentum eclipses typically occur. However, the interaction led to the star's rotation changing significantly. One explanation is that a second, smaller star or brown dwarf is slowly transferring its rotation to the white dwarf over time. This massive object is likely orbiting at a considerable distance, and the star's rotation is the result of the long-term transfer of rotation between the two stars. This interaction provides valuable insight into how stars interact and change rotation, and has important implications to consider when studying rotating stars.

We explore the time complexity of basic operations within a specific mathematical framework, where execution time remains unaffected by input size, based on Leighton's concept. Within this model, we can derive upper bounds on the number of steps required to perform fundamental operations, including creating a random bit, generating random numbers within a specified range, performing divisions and modulo operations, calculating the least significant bit, and determining the inverse of numbers within a specified range. Our key achievements involve proving time efficiency for these operations within this model, and valid examples of programs that validate the feasibility of these operations within a specific time limit, provided that arithmetic operations within a specific time frame are feasible. Within this context, we achieve upper bounds of O(1) for long addition and long multiplication, and O(1/log log N) for long division and long modulo operations. Consequently, this model already embodies nearly optimal sorting algorithms, and aligns well with Feasible Multitape External Storage (FAMES) machines, and P on nearly linear time.

Co-training for session-based recommendations has received increasing attention in recent years, with recent advances focusing on self-supervised learning techniques to enhance recommendation capabilities. Notably, this approach has demonstrated impressive results. Nonetheless, related works have several significant limitations, including poor handling of intra-session user behavior and suboptimal integration of supervision information. To address these issues and push the boundaries further, this paper presents an novel framework called SSLSC, a self-supervised learning method designed to capture session-oriented user behavior more effectively. Specifically, SSLSC employs a self-supervised contrastive approach, which utilizes session-oriented augmentation and sup-norm aggregation to differentiate user sessions and capture user behavior within sessions effectively. Moreover, it proposes a session-representation aggregation method to combine session information and inter-session user behavior and distill intra-session user behavior through attention-based recurrent neural networks. Experiments conducted on real-world datasets demonstrate that SSLSC significantly surpasses the state-of-the-art session-based recommendation approaches in terms of recall metrics and overall performance.

This research presents a novel class of LCD codes, specifically group LCD codes, by utilizing group rings as a mathematical framework. It sets out clear specifications for this new class, establishes a link between group LCD codes and traditional ring LCD codes, and outlines various transformations and coding techniques, including a method for generating group LCD codes from ring LCD codes, dualities, weights, and bounds related to both types of codes. Furthermore, the study introduces group reversible LCD codes, setting their definitions, characteristics, and possible code construction methods, thus expanding upon existing knowledge in the fields of ring LCD codes and reversible LCD codes.

A recent theory proposes an all-encompassing framework for rastering hyperdifferential equations. In this context, we adapt the framework to a specific case by rastering the $q$-Pochhammer differential equation on a graph complex, with the aim of defining hyperdifferential invariants for this equation. By doing so, we establish a novel, graph-based, invariants for solutions of the equation, which have proven particularly beneficial in the study of massless Feynman integrals and non-perturbative effects in quantum field theory and string theory.

A study investigates how different levels of visual processing handle object characteristics.
Previous research found that higher levels of visual processing rely on more category-specific features.
We trained three levels of trained classifiers in a fixed cascade for object categorization.
We discovered that each level processes object properties in a distinct category-independent manner.
These properties fall into two groups: one is orthogonal to the category-specific features and processed at all levels,
while the other is processed only at lower categories and explains the effects of background.
Our findings challenge existing visual processing theories.
They reveal that visual processing is more complex than previously believed and reveal new principles.
They also reveal that visual processing changes as we move from early to late stages,
shifting from stable, orthogonal processing to more category-specific processing.
The discovery of these new principles could lead to significant advancements in understanding how the brain processes visual information.

We explore the impact of correlations on the topological properties of one-dimensional non-Hermitian models. Specifically, we investigate how interactions between constituents affect the topology of models such as the non-Hermitian Aubry-André and Berker models. We demonstrate that the topology can remain stable under specific correlated erratics. However, when the error is random, the system's topology becomes fragile and is disrupted. This phenomenon is explained through the introduction of an auxiliary Hilbert space and the investigation of an generalized non-Hermitian Bloch band theory.

Research on Golay complementary arrays has gained significance due to its applications in various fields like phased arrays, spread spectrum communication, and radar systems. This paper explores the design methods of Golay complementary arrays and a specific type known as low peak-to-average power ratio (PAPR) polyphase Golay complementary arrays. We present the fundamental properties and examples of GCAs of length $N$ with $K$ elements. Our analysis includes the construction of new GCAs using element duplication from shorter length GCAs, as well as the formation of GCAs by combining orthogonal GCAs. The paper also examines Papoulis augmentation and the creation of circular GCAs as well as GCAs with enhanced performance that retain the original length and number of elements but feature reduced PAPR. Specifically, a method is developed to create GCAs with 4 elements and enhanced performance that are applicable for $N \in \{6, 18, 50, 82, 122, 2002\}$.

The significance of the on-shell and off-shell production of the Higgs boson in the four-lepton final state is in-depth explored.  By analyzing the decay channels of Higgs bosons both at resonance and off-resonance, we can derive the width of the Higgs bosons and their connections to other particles.  Additionally, we calculate specific ratios and estimates of the Higgs width, taking into account system uncertainties.  A theoretical framework is also considered in which the coupling of the Higgs boson to other particles is not proportional to their mass.  By comparing our findings with previous research, we highlight potential areas for improvement and expansion in the field.

Incorporating dimensionality reduction techniques into change detection algorithms from the early days has been effective, butSupervised neural networks, such as those using deep learning, struggle with handling high-dimensional data sets, which have limited labels. This research introduces a new, unsupervised method based on Elastic Synapses with Adaptive Modulation (ESAM), which fuses features from multiple layers of a deep neural network to extract essential information, and compares its performance to other change detection methods.

Let $h(G)$ be the minimal number that ensures any coloring of the edges of a graph G with two colors results in at least one monochromatic subgraph that is similar to $H$. In this study, several new, color-based variations of the square of integers are introduced and their Ruzsa sums and Cauchy products investigated.

Quantum interference is a key phenomenon in spin transport, with energy variational effects and valley degrees of freedom also influencing it. We investigated this problem in silicon, using electron microscopy to examine interference patterns and energy variationa effects on spin transport at the atomic level. We created narrow electron channels in silicon by micro-emb implantation and observed interference patterns with different masses and valley degrees of freedom for 0.5 eV electrons using Mott and Okamoto polarimeters respectively. We found that electron implants and magnetic fields both induce symmetry breaking in silicon leading to coherent valley transport, with results from Mott and Okamoto polarimeters agreeing with theoretical predictions. We observed interference patterns and effects of mass and valleys matching with theoretical expectations. We found that implant orientation can control valley interference and mass interference also depends on valley degree of freedom, with findings indicating valley-based interference at the atomic scale in silicon is sensitive to magnetic field strength, electron energy and mass.

Nonconvex optimization is a difficult issue due to its numerous stationary points that are not the global solution. The global solution is even harder to find because there are numerous local minima, and saddle points that are easier to reach from local minima. It has been demonstrated that many practical and complex problems can be resolved using optimization techniques that are not globally convergent. Nonetheless, it is acknowledged that these methods are not always sufficient for all cases. To address this challenge, we introduce a new open-source library called LibOPT that enables the swift development and testing of new soft optimization algorithms. By building upon TensorFlow and PyTorch frameworks, LibOPT integrates various functionalities such as gradient checkpoints, stochastic optimization, and different types of regularizers. Our framework supports end-to-end execution, allowing us to showcase its efficacy through case studies including image restoration, generative adversarial networks, and variational autoencoders. Additionally, we evaluate the newly developed algorithms against established baselines and end-to-end results. Our library can be accessed at https://github.com/quark-corp/libopt.

In this research, we analyze group actions that are both homogeneous and algebraic, focusing on the highest level of transitivity possible. By examining local characteristics of orbits, we establish a crucial criterion for determining the maximum transitivity degree. As a result, we derive a measurable indicator that bounds this transitivity degree from above, applicable to any group acting on any algebraic set. Furthermore, we prove that certain group actions cannot have the maximum possible transitivity degree, using this general criterion. The study specifically looks at actions of special low-rank classical groups, symmetric groups, and the Heisenberg group.

In non-commutative spacetime, the positions of space coordinates do not commute with each other, resulting in the emergence of a new phase where quantum particles exist. We explore the identity crisis of this dual system by analyzing the properties of quantum particles in non-commutative spacetime. By investigating the interaction between these quantum particles and the non-commutative gauge field, we find that the crisis involves the competition between the particles and a magnetic-like field. A phase transition occurs, separating the matter phase, where quantum particles exist, from an embedded quantum Yang-Mills theory, and a non-commutative phase, where the spacetime persists without these quantum particles. Furthermore, we study the thermodynamic behavior of these quantum particles at finite temperature, discovering the annihilation of these quantum particles into a non-commutative gauge field beyond a critical temperature, thus resolving the identity crisis.

We employ the two-photon absorption transient voltage technique to investigate charge transport in high-quality diamond crystals. The initial research focuses on diamond's charge transport properties in the synthetic single-crystal diamond, whereas similar studies have previously been conducted on natural single-crystal diamond. Utilizing this technique allows for the extraction of saturation drift velocity and the product of mobility and lifetime through analysis of both low and high voltage regions. These experiments yielded a saturation drift velocity of 18.4±1 cm/ns and a mobility lifetime product of 3.3±0.1 Vcm for holes, and 14.8±1 cm/ns and a mobility lifetime product of 4.6±0.2 Vcm for electrons. Our results indicate that the mobility lifetime product is electron or hole dependent, contradicting previous findings on diamond's behavior. This novel measurement technique enables the study of diamond's semiconductor characteristics with a high degree of precision.

Social media platforms are subject to a pervasive problem of hate speech, with gender-based violence being a particularly severe form. While models detecting misogyny have been proposed, a comprehensive approach addressing the task in Arabic is still lacking. This study tackles the misrepresentation of Arabic NLP models by introducing a dataset, pre-trained a pre-trained model from scratch, and presents a depth model for identifying and classifying misogyny content across multiple tasks. The data was compiled by gathering various Arabic social media posts from multiple countries, with the dataset then annotated by subject matter experts. Experimental results using our proposed models demonstrate high accuracy in detecting and categorizing Arabic social media content related to misogyny, with a significant improvement of at least 4.77%. Furthermore, the model shows robust performance across different datasets, generalizing well to varying levels of misogyny content.

This study aims to solve open problems regarding the existence and uniqueness of the solution to a class of fractional backward stochastic differential equations (SDEs) under conditions of Lipschitz-type and non-Lipschitz-type conditions. These SDEs differ from traditional ones in that their generators are not directly affected by the sample path of the driving fractional Brownian motion, but rather by the stochastic integral of the generator with respect to the fractional Brownian motion. By assuming certain assumptions, we can establish the existence and uniqueness of the solution to the fractional SDE. Specifically, under conditions of Lipschitz-type, a fixed point argument based on Itô isometry can be used to prove the result. On the other hand, under conditions of non-Lipschitz-type, a fixed point argument can be employed to prove the existence and uniqueness of the solution. Furthermore, we illustrate the practical relevance of the theoretical findings through the example of a financial model.

We introduce a novel framework for predicting a system's future state and determining the optimal control strategy using probability distributions. This approach enhances the resilience of policy selection against uncertainties in the model and the characteristics of external disturbance. The core component of this framework is a universal estimator for the evolution of state probabilities, which also accounts for the effects of control actions and disturbances. The core algorithm arises from combining model prediction standard reinforcement learning techniques, enabling the derivation of the theory of robust dynamic programming and value iteration. The development of estimation methods based on the law of state transitions is a significant contribution, and they demonstrate the ability to accurately capture a system's evolution, even in the presence of minor errors in the control signal. The efficiency of this framework is further highlighted by its ability to circumvent the complications associated with the circular dependency between control and system state, often present in reinforcement learning. The theory is complemented by a set of testing procedures for the proposed model estimator. The performance of the proposed framework is evaluated through the control of a nonlinear system in a 2D space and the analysis of a biological phenomenon, the spread of an infectious disease.

A new framework for combined caching and computation systems has been developed. The framework specifies a memory-computation-hardware system where each device stores a subset of the database and executes functions on cached data inputs to produce outputs. This system optimizes storage, memory usage, and computational complexity. The framework's main innovation is the ability to optimize the trade-off between storage and computation under a specific hardware constraint. The framework reduces to well-known communication complexity problems when specific parameters are set and relates to existing caching and computation schemes. The framework provides a method to evaluate coded caching and distributed computation schemes and is used to establish a connection between linear network coding and linearity in terms of function availability. The framework was successfully applied to solve open problems related to linearity and was used to create efficient linear cache files that were previously thought to be optimal. Additionally, a new storage linearity concept is introduced, which may potentially lead to improved schemes.

We establish the Scott topology on univalent type theory by defining it at the level of axioms. The Scott framework, specifically the Scott separation axiom, the Scott domain topology, and the Scott continuous separation morphisms, can be characterized level-by-level. Furthermore, there exists a natural equivalence between the Scott topology on univalent type theory and the Scott topology on TCF spaces, a concept introduced by Lubin in 2015.

This paper focuses on equipping Fej\'{e}r-G\'{o}m\'{e}z-H\'{o}rvaथ's algorithm with enhanced combinatorial tools to streamline key steps. We also introduce a novel approach for calculating the analytic continuation of Eisenstein series associated with general cuspidal automorphic representations of $GL(n,\mathbb{Q})$, leveraging the Fej\'{e}r-G\'{o}m\'{e}z-H\'{o}rvaथ theta series and building on the Fej\'{e}r-G\'{o}m\'{e}z-H\'{o}rvaथ theta lift and a known identity by Blasius.

This paper explores the challenge of controlling high-dimensional robotic arms in the presence of unanticipated mobile obstacles, which can lead to control issues due to the system's non-convex characteristics. Similar problems have been observed with human-controlled robots, where tasks become complicated by the trade-off between the robot's reach and stability. To address this limitation, our method develops a feedback control strategy that takes into account the robot's configuration, enabling it to manage a wide range of configurations and velocities, and even mobile obstacles changing their own trajectories.

Natural language processing, a crucial field within computer science, focuses on helping computers grasp and interact with human language. Within this field, text summarisation stands out as a significant challenge, and among its various approaches, the extractive method stands out for its simplicity and the coherence of the resulting summaries. Despite its limitations in handling long documents, the extractive method retains value. This study aims to improve extractive text summarisation by exploring the effectiveness of graph-based representations in identifying key sentences. Initial findings suggest the potential of such graph-based representations and the need for further investigation in this area, which, to our knowledge, has been underexplored.

Researchers have suggested that the nonlinear quantum operator framework can model various aspects of Bose-Einstein condensates and their excitation states. These proposed models align well with experimental data, and in this study, we further investigate their mathematical and physical foundations. To develop these models, we utilize an evolution equation method and an internal energy functional approach. Our work demonstrates that these models satisfy key properties such as self-adjointness and positivity. Additionally, by employing the internal energy model, we investigate the long-term stability and stability profiles using both variational methods and a stability profile theory. Our results reveal that all energy levels within this model exceed the ground state energy. Moreover, the continuity of movement from the nonlinear Schrödinger model to the proposed models indicates their ability to represent distinct physical phenomena occurring in BEC systems.

Consider a complete K\"{a}hler manifold (M, ω) and a projective complex variety X, with a compactified form \overline X and an ample line bundle (L|_{\overline X}). Given two non-constant meromorphic mappings f, g: M → ^oX, such that their images are not algebraically equivalent, we define the common value set E(f, g) as the union of all non-algebraically equivalent hyperplanes in the dual space of L that simultaneously contain both f and g. We define s as the supremum of the sum of the counting functions of the counting valuations ν_f and ν_g for all points in f and g, such that s is less than 0, we prove that f and g are distinct as mappings from M to X.

Polynomial systems with non-degenerate solution points are of significant interest due to their extensive applications across various fields. We define the non-degenerate locus of a polynomial system as the set of points where at least one tangent space does not pass through the origin. To determine this non-degenerate locus, we employ a signature-based approach to compute its defining equations, and subsequently, we calculate nearby sample points to estimate its coordinates.

We have measured photon yields at very low momentum ranges for Cu$+$Cu collisions at 200 GeV per nucleon pair, finding that photon measurements align with electronic spectra at higher momenta. However, an interesting deviation at lower momenta suggests the possibility of thermal radiation at the initial stages of the collision. Specifically, the radiative energy loss could account for the observed shift to lower average momentum and may even exceed electron energy loss at the lowest momenta. In the context of the SPS beam energy, our results could be attributed to the formation of a small quark-gluon plasma at the initial stages of the collision.

Achieving a smooth visual effect through anti-aliasing adds complexity to rendering processes, which can be resolved by separating color and light calculations. However, this method has a significant drawback: it causes inconsistencies at line junctions, resulting in an unsightly visual appearance. To rectify this, we propose an innovative two-stage effective space anti-aliasing rendering technique, first by introducing an effective space, then translating it into a real-world space for precise computation. Our approach isolates the issue to pixel scale, making it adaptable to various rendering platforms. Moreover, pre-calculating color variations allows for streamlined rendering, thus eliminating real-time performance constraints. Comparative tests validate the efficacy of our technique in achieving both high visual quality and efficient computing resources.

The multivariate interpolation operator is traditionally constructed using piecewise linear functions to approximate complex functions. In this study, we explore the benefits of the recent transcendental RBF $ \Phi_\alpha = \exp(-\alpha^2 r^2) \sin(\pi r^2) $, where the parameter $ \alpha $ satisfies the condition $ 0 < \alpha < \sqrt{\pi} $, over the entire domain $ \mathbb{R}^d $. We demonstrate that increasing the variation of this RBF results in improved approximation properties. Leveraging $ \Phi_\alpha $, we formulate a novel shape-preserving quasi-interpolation operator that utilizes only the positive values of $ \alpha $. Moreover, we prove that this operator yields second-order global and high-order local convergence rates.

The widespread presence of high-energy photons, extending up to 100 TeV, within the Galaxy's interstellar space, combined with the widespread distribution of cosmic-ray electrons and the substantial magnetic field within the molecular cloud's web suggests that photon emission domains could be created. In addition, the widespread distribution of these domains within the Galaxy's web of molecular clouds and the potential variability of their high-energy photon emission at extragalactic domains, linked to pulsar activity, is discussed. It is also noted that further investigation is required to clarify whether high-energy photon emission at TeV levels originates from the Sagittarius Center.

Understanding the relationship between weather conditions is crucial due to the numerous factors it influences in daily life. Present weather forecasting technologies, although sophisticated, still lack the ability to provide precise numerical predictions. This research addresses this limitation by developing a data enhancement technique that leverages the inherent connections between different weather conditions to improve the performance of a neural network in weather classification tasks. The proposed method involves applying an optimization algorithm to the parameters of a pre-trained GAN (Generative Adversarial Network) to ensure that the generated images are authentic and correspond to existing weather categories. Following this, the research introduces a novel data integration technique that combines traditional weather categories with the enhanced images generated by the network to further improve classification accuracy. This is achieved by incorporating the pre-trained weights from a different architectural structure onto the proposed generative adversial network. To test the efficacy of the proposed method, two distinct convolutional neural network architectures were selected and evaluated against existing weather datasets, including the weather84k (a large-scale, multi-class image dataset) and the weather101 (a widely used weather classification benchmark). The results demonstrate that the proposed method yields a 1.2% and 1.8% increase in the classification accuracy on the weather84k and weather101 datasets, respectively.

Global warming is accelerating at an alarming rate, but public perception lags behind, with many still viewing climate change as a distant issue. We identify a key factor contributing to this disconnect: certain social norms regarding climate change are shaped by various institutions and sectors. During a climate norms conference in Berlin in October 2019, representatives from science, academia, and economics discussed their influence and proposed strategies to realign these norms with the urgency of the crisis. The concept of climate normality serves as a unifying idea, encapsulating the distinct perspectives and responsibilities held by these communities.

This report introduces a real-time, software-based simulation environment for testing and validating online control strategies for flexible multi-fingered grippers. The simulation is based on the dynamics of deformable objects represented via the Koopman operator theory, which is discretized using finite differences. A real-time simulator integrates with a control algorithm that uses model predictive control to grasp and manipulate objects of various types, including a variable stiffness mechanism for improving grip stability. Additionally, the report introduces a novel method for real-time force control, which involves discretizing the gripper's contact area into a grid and estimating the force at each point.

Our analysis reveals that the Organic Evolution equation, a stochastic process, generalizes the Traditional Ordinary Differential Equations. It incorporates Brownian motion into the flow along a manifold, and when this motion's amplitude shrinks to zero, it reduces to the original equation. Moreover, when this model is applied to a negative gradient descent on an organic loss function, it encompasses both a Traditional and a Generalized Kullback-Leibler divergence.

The high-redshift radio source J2102+6015, with a significant neutral gas outflow, has been observed at a remarkable distance of z = 4.575. By analyzing spectra from the KMOS-3D spectrograph at a high spatial resolution of ~1.5", we were able to precisely measure the source's line of sight recession velocity and an unusually low velocity dispersion of ~210 km/s. Furthermore, we identified 10 emission lines and determined the source's extinction value of A(V) = 0.43 ± 0.11. This allows for the reconstruction of the source's intrinsic spectrum and an estimation of its star formation law, which suggests that the source is in an early stage of high-intensity star formation. This is the first high-z radio source to exhibit a low velocity dispersion and a high gas outflow rate simultaneously. Its properties are consistent with a young star-forming galaxy with extended star formation timescales. This novel property may be essential for a young galaxy to develop into an extremely massive galaxy.

Lung cancer accounts for a high number of cancer deaths worldwide and necessitates an accurate and efficient diagnosis and treatment. This work contributes to the improvement of lung cancer diagnosis and prediction by developing an innovative system that integrates text and visual information from medical scans. This system uses clinical texts and patient health data to refine the accuracy of predicting the progression of lung cancer, while cutting-edge deep learning techniques analyze the text and medical images to identify relevant patterns. The results show that the proposed system significantly outperforms current state-of-the-art methods, achieving exceptional accuracy rates of 82% to 89% in forecasting the progression of lung cancer.

In certain tasks, reinforcement learning can be inefficient due to sparse rewards. 
Using natural language to describe game states provides rich information that could help overcome this limitation. 
Though using natural language in reinforcement learning appears promising, it poses significant technical difficulties. 
This paper aims to clarify the overview of natural language use in reinforcement learning by reviewing existing literature and exploring current approaches. 
It will analyze the utilization of natural language in reinforcement learning, the datasets employed for training, and the architectures used for processing, as well as evaluate performance based on standard evaluation metrics. 
Finally, this paper will discuss potential future research directions in this field.

A novel approach combining machine learning and astrophysics is introduced, 
where the cosmic density power spectrum is reconstructed using 4,299 absorbed quasar 
spectra and 502 control points, at redshifts ranging from 2.2 to 3.5. A Swin 
Transformer, used in image processing, is adapted to analyze low-resolution spectral 
data, effectively capturing both local and global features. A Stepwise Feature 
Masking technique is employed to determine the significance of absorbed quasar 
spectra in reconstructing the density power spectrum. A cross-validation method 
facilitates the direct learning of the relationship between the absorbed quasar 
spectra and the cosmic density power spectrum. A precise reconstruction of the 
linear density power spectrum is achieved, with the estimated error closely 
matching the theoretical prediction, and a high-level reconstruction of the 
nonlinear density power spectrum is also successfully obtained. This research 
highlights the tremendous potential of a direct machine learning method and its 
significance for cosmological research. Additionally, the features extracted from 
the spectra provide valuable insights into the distribution of matter at the 
cosmic scale and the evolution of quasar host galaxies. This research signifies 
the significant potential of machine learning in cosmological research.

This research explores certain modules over the Lie algebras of differential operators, specifically those that are free over the algebra of univariate polynomials. We establish criteria to identify such free modules and further, we prove that these free structures comprise the complete set. Building on existing theories, an alternative approach is used to study modules whose sections vanish at the origin. Initially, such structures were characterized as a subset of general Lie algebras of differential operators. Here, it is shown that for a module to be U(h)-free, it must satisfy the condition. Additionally, a new classification theorem is developed. Finally, the study considers the case where the weight is zero and proves that the module is isomorphic to u(h)-Casimirs under this condition.

Social media sentiment analysis on platforms like Twitter offers valuable insights
into various trends, enabling businesses and organizations to effectively
communicate and adapt their strategies. With over 278 million active users
generating over 300 million posts daily in just four languages, understanding
Twitter data requires processing unstructured text containing social media
specific characteristics. After initial data cleaning, we employ Long Short-Term
Memory models to classify Twitter sentiments accurately. Our model achieves
exceptional results with 81.68% accuracy on combined datasets, demonstrating
improvements of 10% to 20% over existing methods.

Recent breakthroughs with open-domain dialogue systems have drawn significant interest from the industry and academia, exemplified by applications like Replika and Amazon Alexa. Although prior research has yielded impressive results, they fall short in delivering truly natural and unbounded conversations. A major limitation of these systems is their narrow knowledge, but a major advancement in language models, such as GPT-3, has now made it possible to create more engaging and natural systems. We've developed a new method for designing open-domain dialogue systems with a specific role in mind, such as simulating GPT-4's conversational abilities, by fine-tuning on role-specific datasets and using a knowledge-conditioned text generation approach. Our constructed system exhibits remarkable similarity to GPT-4 in both qualitative and quantitative evaluations. Additionally, we've identified new datasets for role-based conversational systems, making them publicly available, and plan to release them alongside the complete code in this project's repository.

New gravitational wave observatories will likely be capable of detecting background signals generated by the collective effects of numerous sources.  These signals can span a variety of frequencies, and a comprehensive understanding of their characteristics will be essential for interpreting future observational data.  Research has shown that it's possible to describe such backgrounds in terms of the individual wave populations that generate them.  Focusing on binary neutron star mergers, scientists have previously determined the characteristics of several gravitational wave bands;  however, they overlooked the contribution of the final frequency band, known as the memory band.  This study will now investigate the properties of signals produced by these mergers within the memory band and develop a method for distinguishing between different types of sources that generate it.  Because the memory persists long after the main signals cease, the duration of these signals is significantly extended, and their dynamics are entirely distinct from the earlier and later bands.  Because of the memory's continuous state, its behavior is highly sensitive to the intricate relationship between the neutron stars' orbital evolution and the neutron stars' internal composition.  Graphs will be provided to aid in further investigation of the composition-dependent source distribution expected from the memory band and to compare it with the dominant second-order source.

A successful case of baryon generation through the leptonic process requires the existence of massive neutrinos, whose origins are unclear. In this study, we show that the required neutrino masses can be generated at the scale of a phase transition in a theory of supergravity by breaking the masses of the super Yang Mills theory, which occurs at the scale of several PeV. This theory transition also produces gravitational waves with detectable strength by LIGO and VIGO and creates numerous microscopic black holes. These black holes are stable due to the slow emission of gravitational waves and may be found within our galaxy or potentially within our solar system. This model offers an explanation for the origins of neutrino masses, dark matter, and possible modifications to hydrogen's 21cm spectrum due to the interaction of microscopic black holes with interstellar hydrogen atoms.

Recent research has expanded the application of neural network models, particularly those that incorporate symbolic elements, to tackle complex causal inquiries. This paper builds upon that research by integrating these neural network models into a signaling game to simulate a dynamic communication system between an encoder and a decoder. In this game, the encoder uses observed state information and communicates with the decoder through a symbol generated by a neural network, while the decoder based on received symbols and its own knowledge predicts a target variable. This model explores how meaningful communication can naturally arise between two agents in order to predict a target variable, while also developing a method for training both agents to simultaneously optimize their performance. Through applications on both synthetic and real-world datasets for causal inference, the results demonstrate that the system's behavior on out-of-distribution data is consistent with the theory of differential input-output independence.

In the field of Natural Language Processing, term prediction is a crucial task. 
Researchers have proposed various strategies to tackle this problem, including using 
statistical models and neural network-based methods. The challenge lies in 
handling sparse terms that are unlikely to appear in training data. The 
information from similar terms can assist in predicting unseen terms. This paper 
introduces an hybrid model combining the strength of Maximum Entropy estimates and 
information from sparse terms. The model is evaluated on three term prediction datasets 
within the Microbloging social media platform. Experimental results demonstrate 
that the proposed method outperforms existing solutions.

Session-oriented recommendations have seen significant advancement in the last few years, with researchers focusing on understanding user sessions as sequences of actions. Typically, the session embedding is calculated by taking the sum of individual action embeddings. However, this method assumes that all session actions contribute equally to the session embedding, which is not always the case. In reality, some actions are more representative of the session than others and should have a greater impact on the session embedding. To address this issue, we propose using candidate rank embeddings to dynamically weigh the contribution of each session action. Furthermore, to avoid a common pitfall where recommendation systems only suggest similar items, we developed a two-stage model. The first stage aims to identify a broad area of action types applicable to the user session, while the second stage selects a specific action type and ranks candidate actions within that category to produce a diverse and personalized recommendation list. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of our model.

In recent years, there's been significant interest in the behavior of microscopic agents that self-propel, which is particularly so given its connection to active matter. This interest has led to the formation of complexes known as colloidal molecules, consisting of multiple particles that are held together by specific interactions. The present study focuses on a particular type of three-particle molecule, specifically one that's symmetric, and examines how it behaves in a environment with an activity gradient. Through theoretical calculations, it's discovered that molecules with specific interaction patterns tend to move in a way that's analogous to Brownian motion within a effective potential that depends on their interaction strengths. As their patterns of interaction change, molecules begin to rotate in a purposeful manner. For molecules that exhibit specific interaction characteristics, it's observed that they rotate in a way that allows them to move forward, while those with different interaction patterns move backward. The speed of these molecules can be controlled by adjusting their composition, which also affects their movement speed in a manner comparable to changes in their physical properties. To better understand this motion, the study employs both an analytical method based on a specific theoretical framework, as well as a specific imaging technique, which provides further insight into the mechanisms at play.

Our research tackles the complexities of simulating single-phase flow in fractured porous media. We've developed a 3D discrete fracture-matrix (DFM) model using an unstructured mesh, which facilitates the application of a 19-node tetrahedral Mimetic Finite Element method. This 3D approach builds upon a previously established 2D technique. Our work addresses a critical challenge in the literature, involving the conformal fitting of fractures within a mesh. To verify our method's efficacy, we performed a series of testing procedures, including verification of verifiable test cases and comparison of results with test cases from the literature. Additionally, we evaluated our method's performance under various grid sizes, frame of reference, and fracture orientations. Ultimately, we successfully applied our method to realistic scenarios, such as Karst systems and complex networks of fractures, achieving promising results.

This study introduces an innovative approach called Centroid-Based Point Set Registration (cBPSR), an original algorithm designed for colliding a swarm of drones while maintaining formation. cBPSR not only serves as an original method but also as an alternative to the existing SOFT formation collision avoidance system. The key difference lies in cBPSR'sKmeans++ implementation, as opposed to SOFT's Kmeans. Kmeans++ is a enhanced version of Kmeans that efficiently selects initial centroids, enhancing algorithm performance. To determine the optimal initial clusters, we developed a virtual scenario where each cluster represents a specific time frame and drone position, allowing us to calculate formation deviations from the initial cluster centroid. The experiment involved a simulated scenario with a hexagonal formation of 7 drones, and the results show that initial cluster selection significantly impacts overall analysis outcomes. Additionally, we discovered that using Kmeans on this type of data is an inefficient choice.

In graph theory, the Seidel matrix is a valuable tool used to analyze graph spectra. This paper delves into the spectral range and vertex energies of the Seidel matrix specifically for chain graphs. The research finds that the eigenvalues of the Seidel matrix for a chain graph with a symmetric partition are limited to at most three distinct values. The largest eigenvalue is identified as the highest root of a provided polynomial, while the eigenvalues -1 and the smallest eigenvalue $\lambda_1$ are identified. The paper then calculates the total and Larmor energies of the graph in terms of the smallest eigenvalue and its algebraic multiplicity.

We formulate and resolve a optimal control problem known as the mean-field optimal control problem for stochastic differential equations with delay driven by fractional Brownian motion. To address this problem, we first convert it into a family of optimal control problems driven by fractional Brownian motion. By leveraging the properties of this motion and employing techniques including variational methods and time discretization, we establish necessary and sufficient conditions for optimality. These conditions confirm the existence of unique solutions to the associated two-point boundary value problems derived from the maximum principle. As result, we prove the convergence of discrete approximations to these solutions. To demonstrate the practical application of our results, we provide a numerical example showcasing an explicit explicit solution.

We investigate a class of non-self-adjoint Dirac operators with periodic structure, focusing on elliptical finite bands of their spectra. The set of all such elliptical bands forms a 3D manifold, and we define energy functions that map from the space of triples consisting of wavenumber, ellipses major axis, and minor axis to the reals. The properties of these energy functions are examined in detail.

As the demand for wireless communication within roadside units (RSUs) increases, they often struggle to meet it all alone, leading to a necessity for network expansion through vehicle relays. By incorporating vehicular ad hoc networks (VANETs) with RSUs and relays, we can enhance the overall mobility data traffic management. We've developed a two-layer VANET model that combines an optical backbone with an wireless access layer, where we've studied the backhaul and access link behaviors using Markov chains, random process, and queuing models. With this, we've analyzed key performance indicators, including vehicle and RSU inventory, vehicle queuing, optical and wireless load, and system throughput, within both steady-state and transient conditions. We've also compared our proposed model with a conventional approach, where every RSU is connected directly to the backbone, to demonstrate the beneficial aspects of this new model in scenarios with high traffic on the access layer but manageable load on the backbone.

The goal of automatically identifying and marking low-quality content on Wikipedia articles is to facilitate targeted interventions through automated systems and human editors. We developed a novel automatic labeling system by examining the behavior patterns of the editorial team across the entire Wikipedia archive. This multi-class classifier, trained on the entire historical dataset, accurately identifies low-quality content without necessitating the labeling of new articles. We conducted an experiment by randomly selecting 2,000 articles in English and manually assessing their quality. Our system's performance was evaluated, comparing the predicted labels of these randomly chosen articles with the manual labels provided by researchers. We observed that the model's performance remained stable during this testing phase. We anticipate this labeling system to enhance the efficiency of human editors and research studies focused on the quality of the entire Wikipedia corpus.

Understanding the underlying cause-and-effect relationships of machine learning models is crucial for their broad acceptance in high-stakes fields. Developing methods to transfer knowledge from black-box models, whose internal workings are unknown, to white-box models, whose structure is visible, is necessary. Existing techniques typically require access to specific data points and their responses from both models. However, these methods are impractical in real-world applications where such access is limited or non-existent. Our approach overcomes these limitations by testing predictions from black-box models with artificially created images to understand their response patterns, and then using this information to train a new, white-box model that can accurately predict their behavior without needing input from the original black-box model. This white-box model can then be used to transfer its insights to a white-box target, enabling a more effective transfer of knowledge.

We investigate T-duality for twisted cylinders, extending prior research that covered simple cylinders and Riemannian homogeneous spaces with isometries. Our results reveal that T-duality preserves the holonomy form and white noise form. Furthermore, distinct T-duals of a single twisted cylinder can yield non-isometric metric spaces. Our approach leverages the metric formalism developed by St\'ankiwicz for twisted circles, leveraging their association with Riemannian R-homomorphisms. Our analysis leverages existing knowledge of R-twisted twisted cylinders, drawing from work by R. Rejaie and D. Reijns.

A well-known Co-Imitation training method uses data from a single successful expert show to teach robots complex tasks. This approach relies on the assumption that multiple agents learn to replicate the expert's actions, even though the expert is only present in a single interaction. As a result, the majority of robot interactions in a training set are based on the actions of other agents, rather than the expert. Inspired by this, we explore the implications of training on data generated by other agents, rather than experts. We find that, despite the absence of an actual expert in these interactions, the performance of the trained robots remains comparable to that of the expert when tested. This suggests a viable means of scaling up Co-Imination training. We propose a system for collecting data, the Field Study Protocol Data Set, and evaluate our methods using data from this set, showing that Co-Imination training on this dataset yields agents that are both robust to variations in agent sizes and generalise well to unknown environments.

This paper investigates properties of Prediction-Accuracy Confirmation codes, a type of universal lossless compression, focusing on the $\ell_1$ metric's role in their performance. The research derives new, precise formulas for the PAC distribution and demonstrates that the $\ell_1$ metric yields tighter bounds on its performance. The $\ell_1$ metric is shown to be equivalent to the maximum deviation from the true distribution over all possible outcomes. This code is further shown to be a universal estimator with a prediction risk bounded at a constant times $\log(N)/n$ when the dataset size is $n$ and the number of possible outcomes is $N$. Additionally, the calculation of PAC codes is found to be a computationally feasible task with a time complexity of $O(N^n \log(N^n))$. Finally, the performance of PAC codes based on the $\ell_1$ metric is evaluated through simulation and compared to other methods, such as the maximum likelihood estimator, revealing significant improvements, up to a factor of 3 in some cases, in terms of prediction risk.

Understanding how objects interact is a fundamental aspect of perception that has significant implications for advanced AI applications like driving and robotics. However, extracting object interaction data from video footage is a challenging task, particularly when point cloud sequences are used, which typically offer limited depth information and low spatial resolution. Our research introduces Solid, a novel system that can accurately track and regenerate object interactions within 3D point cloud sequences. By focusing solely on visible interactions within the scene, rather than attempting to render a complete 3D environment, our method simplifies the extraction of interaction data and allows for the recovery of high-resolution object meshes. By evaluating our approach on a new dataset, SolidOutdoors, which features outdoor scenes with humans manipulating objects, we found Solid to outperform baseline methods and even a model trained on indoor data in terms of accuracy.

This study classifies C-groups with a specific structure - non-crystallographic, rank 4, and interleaving number 2. A total of 12 groups fitting this description were identified and categorized. Furthermore, the number of distinct arithmetic families within this set was determined.

A novel, end-efferator pose estimation system using a robot-depth camera has been developed, which avoids the need for external markers. An optimization technique was implemented to automatically adjust the camera's intrinsic and extrinsic parameters as well as end-effector parameters, while estimated pose was validated with high-precision external feedback from external markers. Our approach demonstrates the capability to learn camera parameters, which contributes to reducing overfitting and improves generalization, ultimately resulting in accurate and efficient pose estimation with minimal external feedback.

Identifying the precise impact of a new therapy can be challenging due to the potential interference from concurrent treatments and the limited availability of control subjects necessary to establish a direct comparison. Present, an alternative strategy is proposed that utilizes K-Nearest-Neighbors to pinpoint and remove therapy interference data points without a control group. Empirical verification through simulated data and real-world breast cancer survival data indicates that Present effectively distinguishes and isolates therapy interference. Moreover, NKNN variation of Present enables a direct comparison between a control group and data points influenced by the new therapy through an established difference-in-distance metric to determine individual therapy effects.

Calculations of neutrino production within the sun have been conducted, taking into account the impact of Dark Matter annihilation facilitated by pseudoscalar interactions. In certain conditions, the efficiency of neutrino emission can be significantly elevated, surpassing the standard electromagnetic process. This phenomenon holds potential for explaining the long-standing problem associated with two-reaction equilibrium in solar plasma. Furthermore, the existence of such Dark Matter could potentially be investigated through observations of solar neutrinos and astrophysical objects, potentially enabling direct detection at facilities like LXe based detectors or the International Linear Collider, along with other experimental setups.

I've developed, called ShapePipe, a comprehensive pipeline for the precise measurement of galaxy shapes, specifically ellipticity and orientation. This pipeline was utilized to analyze Unions data, ultimately supplementing the Cosmic Flow Investigation Survey's echo survey. By applying ShapePipe to 51,314 Unions galaxies with a redshift of up to 0.009, high redshift cutoff excluded, a total of 45,421 galaxies passed its quality control filters with corresponding coefficients of variation ranging from 0.0003 to 0.001. The application of these shape measurements enabled the calculation of shear two-point correlation functions with a magnitude of 10^-3, which was then employed to verify the detection of weak lensing with a confidence margin of 4-sigma. Additionally, the application of these shape measurements enabled the detection of alignment with unassociated radio sources at an improved significance level compared to previous studies. These results showcase the utility of the Unions dataset and ShapePipe for performing cosmological and morphological studies.

We establish enhanced arithmetical estimation techniques for certain infinite sequences, including those in a given value and the fractional parts of nα. Leveraging these methods, we derive new equidistribution theorems that build upon existing Kronecker-Weyl type outcomes and resolve an open problem posed by Huang and Li. Moreover, we present enhanced results on the approximation of numbers by rational values, which surpass a significant result by Balaská et al.
We have found a positive response to a k-rational implies k-Du Bois query by demonstrating that every k-rational singular point in a local complete variate is indeed k-Du Bois.

We've discovered direct experimental evidence for the relationship between Berezinskii-Kosterlitz-Thouless (BKT) correlations and a 3D physics phenomenon, which emerges from a single model that combines these two areas of study. By applying external magnetic fields to a spin pyramid spin chain known as [NiPy$_{1-x}$Mn$_x$]$_2$O$_3$, we observed a transition in spin correlations due to the continuous change in magnetic field. We measured how these spin correlations were affected and found that an critical point at which they suddenly changed was influenced by the doping level of Mn ions in the chain. We believe our discovery brings new insights into the study of field-induced BKT correlations and their potential applications in the creation of spin-based electronic devices.

This study investigates the feasibility of axion and sterile neutrino models coexisting, specifically within the context of cosmological density closure. To address potential issues with generating sufficient axion dark matter through traditional "misalignment" production in high-temperature universe models, we propose a framework where axion dark matter is predominantly produced after a transition from a sterile neutrino model to the present universe's density model. Our analysis demonstrates that existing constraints on sterile neutrinos can be satisfied while substantial amounts of axion dark matter can still be generated. Furthermore, we explore scenarios where axions are directly constrained by their interaction with nuclei, and we find that a specific combination of sterile neutrino and axion parameters could account for the entire density of the present universe's model.

The minimal amount of basis elements needed to represent a given quantum state is known as its decompositional rank, with applications in quantum algorithms and approximations. The depth of quantum circuits is limited by the associated state's decompositional rank. Currently, the rank in terms of computational basis states is known to be at least exponential in the square of the circuit depth. This research improves the minimum limit on the rank for stabilizer circuits with phases, by demonstrating that the dual exponential bound applies when the circuit size is sufficiently large relative to the depth and angle, thereby approaching the general bound. Additionally, we show that certain non-stabilizer circuits are at least required to have a higher decompositional rank in order to reach specific target angles even at the fullest available available basis elements.

This research investigates the behavior of a complex form of essence model within two theories of holographic dark energy, namely typical and density radius.  The authors examine how this model relates to current cosmological observations, calculating key parameters such as the equation of state, state parameter, and density.  The study demonstrates that this model can effectively reproduce the observed acceleration in the universe, and that it aligns with current data from supernovae, baryon acoustic oscillations, low-redshift cosmic chronometers, and Planck results.  Additionally, the authors apply Tomita's theorem to analyze the stability of the complex essence model, and establish constraints on parameters for both theories, finding results consistent with the predicted properties of holographic dark energy.  Furthermore, the authors assess the finiteness of certain parameters and conduct a likelihood analysis, obtaining a Hubble constant value of 71.26 ± 2.92, which is in line with other studies.  The findings also suggest that this model exhibits a finite future finiteness.

Data analysis from four $K$2 plates of the LAMOST Time-domain Survey was completed, with an focus on variable star detection. The survey's initial phase used four redundant plates for enhanced star identification and frequency range of 15149-78976 $\AA$. A total of 21936 profiles of single objects were created, resulting in an average 12.6% rejection rate of inadequate spectra, leaving 21242 valid profiles. The study found 1008 variable stars and single-eclipsing binary systems, with an average exposure time of 810 s, of which 86.5% were new discoveries. The remaining 12240 stationary objects were also analyzed, with nearly 60% showing multiple distinct sources, largely attributed to cosmic-ray impact rejection, with true variable content estimated at approximately 4%. The study found about 17% of the objects to be self-absorbed, limiting the survey's full potential, with varying effective bandwidths across the objects. The study found approximately 17% of the objects to be self-absorption affected, while its impact on variable star yields is estimated at approximately 7%, with varying effective bandwidths across the objects. The study found about 17% of the objects to be self-absorption affected, with its impact on variable star yields estimated at approximately 7%.

This paper explores the underlying mechanism for generating random numbers in an SRAM, taking advantage of the variability present in true random number creators. We identified that SRAM supply voltage underscaling can effectively serve as a reliable source of entropy by inducing unstable oscillations in SRAM memory cells. We name this technique the True Random Number Creator using Supply Voltage Underscaling, which we abbreviate as TuRaN. We put forth TuRaN as a novel approach to enhance the efficiency of TRCs while minimizing their size and area. Furthermore, TuRaN's design remains straightforward and straightforward to implement. It is compact in logic since it requires no additional components beyond the shift register. We Nverified the accuracy of TuRaN through SPICE simulations using a 65nm memory cell and confirmed its functionality through HSPICE simulations. HSPICE simulations were also used to evaluate the impact of varying parameters on the final output. We assessed the quality of the random numbers generated by TuRaN through statistical tests including NIST, DIEHARD, and ARSeC. We further analyzed the performance of TuRaN under supply voltage underscaling and its sensitivity to process and supply voltage fluctuations. We further optimized the design by determining the optimal shift register length based on an estimated supply voltage margin. We found that the ideal length of the shift register is 32 bits. A preliminary design of a single-electron resistor switch has been developed using an electron-attached insulating organic molecule, which acts as a single-electron tunneling single-electron transistor. The key distinction between this new type of switch and traditional single-electron transistor switches is that the former utilizes a single electron to operate, whereas the latter requires two electrons. Preliminary simulations have shown that these organic molecules can act as effective switches, having a Coulomb blockade energy that is two for one of the capture electron's activation energy. The present study focuses on designing these molecular switches, which are based on single electron transistors, which have a potential to be miniaturized and integrated into nanoscale applications. The present design, which uses an electron-attached molecule, has a for one activation energy that is approximately 50% lower than the two electrons switch. The present design, which uses an electron-attached molecule, has a for one activation energy that is approximately 50% lower than the two electrons switch.
